High peak HR during the trajectory phase may indicate ongoing instability (pain, sepsis, low output, AF with RVR) associated with renal hypoperfusion. Max captures acute stress better than mean.

Late peak tachycardia can be a leading indicator of deterioration (shock, infection, arrhythmia) that increases AKI risk via reduced effective renal perfusion. Still indirect without concurrent BP/CO data.

Bradycardia may reflect conduction issues or pacing/sedation effects early after surgery and is not specific for renal injury. Minimum HR can matter if it reflects low cardiac output, but early period is noisy.
Low HR could indicate conduction disease or over-sedation and only indirectly relates to renal perfusion unless associated with low output. As an isolated feature it is a weak predictor of AKI.

Late bradycardia may reflect conduction failure, excessive beta-blockade, or low-output states that can reduce renal blood flow and contribute to AKI. The minimum captures potentially harmful low-rate episodes better than mean.
Heart rate measurement frequency is routine ICU monitoring and does not represent a renal mechanism. In the immediate post-op period it provides little discriminatory value for AKI.
Measurement counts largely reflect standard monitoring rather than physiology. It is not specific for renal hypoperfusion or tubular injury.
Even late, pulse measurement frequency is typically continuous/standard and not a meaningful predictor of creatinine rise. It is a behavioral/monitoring artifact rather than a causal AKI signal.

Mean inspired O2/anesthetic gas exposure in the immediate post-op window has no direct mechanistic link to AKI and is largely routine ventilator/anesthesia management. Any association would be confounded by overall illness severity rather than renal perfusion.

High O2 exposure may correlate with severity of respiratory/cardiac dysfunction and oxidative stress, but it is not an established direct driver of post-cardiac surgery AKI. In 0–12h, transient high FiO2 is common, so prognostic value is limited.

Low O2 delivery (proxy for hypoxemia) could contribute to renal ischemia, but minimum O2 agent value is an indirect and noisy marker compared with direct oxygenation/hemodynamic measures. Early post-op fluctuations are common, so cap relevance in 0–12h.
Measurement frequency reflects documentation/monitoring intensity rather than a physiologic mechanism for AKI. In the immediate post-op period, frequent recording is routine.
O2 agent measurement frequency is primarily a care-process marker and not a direct predictor of renal injury. At 13–24h it may weakly reflect ongoing instability but remains nonspecific.
More frequent O2 agent measurements late may indicate persistent respiratory failure/acuity, which can correlate with AKI risk via shock/low perfusion. Still a behavioral proxy, so kept low.
Nitrous oxide exposure has no established direct relationship to postoperative AKI in this context. Mean use in 0–12h mainly reflects anesthetic practice rather than renal risk.
Peak nitrous oxide administration is not a recognized trigger for renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity after cardiac surgery. Any association would be indirect and likely confounded.
Minimum nitrous oxide level is clinically uninformative for kidney outcomes and largely reflects whether/when the agent was discontinued. No meaningful physiologic link to AKI.
Frequency of N2O recording is a documentation artifact and does not represent a renal injury mechanism. In 0–12h it is routine peri-anesthesia monitoring.
N2O measurement frequency after surgery is uncommon and, when present, reflects care patterns rather than kidney physiology. Not a specific indicator of impending AKI.
Late measurement frequency of N2O is not a plausible direct predictor of creatinine rise and is likely sparse/noisy. Retained as minimal importance.
Mean air (carrier gas) administration is routine ventilator/anesthesia management and has no direct causal pathway to AKI. It is largely redundant with other respiratory support variables.
Maximum air delivery is not a recognized marker of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. In early post-op care it mainly reflects ventilator settings rather than kidney risk.
Minimum air delivery is not clinically meaningful for AKI prediction and is dominated by routine transitions in respiratory support. No established association with postoperative creatinine rise.
Measurement frequency is a care-process proxy and provides little specific information about renal injury risk. Early post-op recording frequency is standard-of-care.

Measurement frequency of delivered air/anesthetic carrier gas is a documentation/monitoring artifact and not a physiologic driver of AKI. At most it reflects routine ventilator/anesthesia charting rather than renal risk.
Counts of air/anesthetic carrier measurements do not reflect renal perfusion, nephrotoxicity, or kidney injury. More frequent recording is not a specific marker of impending AKI.

Volatile anesthetic exposure can influence blood pressure and renal perfusion indirectly, but mean dose in the immediate post-op window is not a strong or specific AKI predictor. Collinearity: extremes would better capture hypotension-related insult than the mean.

Higher peak isoflurane may correlate with deeper anesthesia and hypotension, which can reduce renal perfusion, but this is indirect and confounded by intraop management. In 0–12h, transient anesthetic effects are common, so relevance is capped.
Minimum isoflurane largely reflects weaning/off anesthesia and is not a marker of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. It has little mechanistic link to subsequent creatinine rise.
Measurement frequency reflects charting intensity rather than physiologic exposure or renal injury. It is not a direct predictor of AKI.
How often isoflurane is recorded is a behavioral/monitoring proxy and not a renal mechanism. Continued measurement may reflect ongoing sedation but is nonspecific for AKI risk.
Recording frequency of isoflurane does not quantify hemodynamic instability or kidney injury and is highly practice-dependent. It provides minimal incremental signal for creatinine_ratio.

Mean SvO2 reflects global oxygen delivery/consumption balance and can relate to perfusion, but early post-CPB values are often transient and treatment-responsive. Collinearity: the minimum SvO2 better captures hypoperfusion episodes relevant to AKI.

Sustained lower SvO2 can indicate inadequate cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion, but the mean can mask critical low episodes. The minimum SvO2 is typically the more pathologic aggregation for AKI risk.

High SvO2 is generally not a direct trigger for AKI and may reflect high FiO2, sedation, or impaired extraction rather than renal hypoperfusion. In the immediate post-op period it is especially nonspecific.

Maximum SvO2 does not capture hypoperfusion risk and is weakly related to renal injury mechanisms. It is often driven by ventilatory/oxygenation settings and sedation rather than kidney-relevant physiology.
Low SvO2 episodes suggest low cardiac output/systemic hypoperfusion, a recognized pathway to postoperative AKI. In 0–12h this is common and may be transient, so importance is conservatively capped.

A low SvO2 nadir in 13–24h indicates persistent or recurrent inadequate oxygen delivery/low output state, strongly linked to renal hypoperfusion and AKI after cardiac surgery. This trajectory-phase signal is more prognostic than early transient lows.
More frequent SvO2 checks can reflect clinician concern for shock/low output, which is indirectly related to AKI risk. However it is a behavioral proxy and early post-op monitoring is often routine.

Increased SvO2 measurement frequency may indicate ongoing hemodynamic instability or concern for low output, indirectly associated with AKI. Still, it is not a physiologic mechanism and is practice-dependent.

Measurement frequency of SvO2 is mainly a proxy for clinician concern about low cardiac output/shock, which can predispose to AKI. As a _measured feature it is not a physiologic value and should be kept low.

Maintenance IV volume relates indirectly to renal perfusion and fluid overload, but early post-op fluids are routine and highly protocolized. Mean volume is also less informative than extremes for AKI-relevant insults.

Ongoing maintenance fluids may reflect evolving hemodynamics and attempts to support perfusion, but mean volume is a nonspecific management variable. Extremes (e.g., high max suggesting aggressive resuscitation) would better capture pathology.

Later maintenance fluid requirements can correlate with instability or poor intake, but mean volume remains a weak, nonspecific driver of AKI compared with hemodynamics, urine output, or creatinine trends. Prefer extremes to avoid collinearity.

A high maximum maintenance IV volume in the immediate post-op window can indicate aggressive fluid administration for hypotension/low output, which is linked to AKI risk. However, in 0–12h this is often transient and routine, so capped at 3.

A high max maintenance IV volume during 13–24h may reflect persistent hemodynamic compromise or ongoing resuscitation, both associated with AKI. Still indirect and treatment-driven rather than a direct renal biomarker.

A high max maintenance IV volume close to the outcome suggests ongoing instability/low effective circulating volume or attempts to treat it, which strongly correlates with subsequent AKI in post-cardiac surgery patients. This extreme is more informative than mean/min for capturing acute insult.

Low minimum maintenance IV volume early post-op is usually protocol/line-management related and not a reliable marker of renal hypoperfusion. The minimum is less likely than the maximum to capture AKI-relevant pathology.
Minimum maintenance IV volume is a weak and nonspecific indicator and may reflect transitions in care rather than physiology. It is unlikely to add AKI-specific signal beyond max volume/hemodynamics.

A low minimum maintenance IV volume late post-op is not a dependable proxy for renal perfusion and is often driven by orders/feeding status. It is less pathophysiologically linked to AKI than high-volume extremes or direct renal/hemodynamic measures.
Measurement frequency is primarily documentation/ordering behavior and routine in the immediate post-op period. As a _measured feature it provides minimal physiologic information for AKI prediction.
How often maintenance IV volume is recorded is largely workflow-related and not a direct mechanism for AKI. At most it weakly reflects acuity, so kept at 1.
Recording frequency of maintenance IV volume is not a physiologic marker and is heavily influenced by nursing/EMR practices. It should remain low to avoid spurious behavioral signal.

Having PAP systolic measured suggests a PA catheter and concern for cardiopulmonary hemodynamics/low output, which relates to AKI risk. As a measured/availability proxy (not the value), and in 0–12h, it should stay low.
Continued PAP monitoring implies ongoing hemodynamic concern that can be associated with renal hypoperfusion and AKI. Still a behavioral proxy rather than a direct physiologic predictor.

PAP monitoring persisting into 25–36h may indicate unresolved shock/right heart dysfunction, which can contribute to AKI. However, because this is only a measured indicator (not PAP values), importance remains limited.

Measurement frequency of PA diastolic pressure mainly reflects monitoring intensity rather than renal physiology. Early post-op (0–12h) hemodynamic monitoring is routine and not specific for AKI risk.
How often PAP diastolic is recorded is a weak behavioral proxy for acuity and is not a direct driver of AKI. In 13–24h this remains largely monitoring practice rather than kidney-specific signal.

Increased frequency of PAP diastolic measurements late (25–36h) may indicate ongoing shock/heart failure evaluation, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still, it is a monitoring-intensity proxy rather than a physiologic insult.
CVP measurement frequency reflects clinician concern/monitoring and is common immediately after cardiac surgery. It is not itself a physiologic determinant of creatinine rise.

More frequent CVP checks in 13–24h can signal persistent hemodynamic instability or volume management challenges, indirectly linked to AKI. As a _measured feature it remains a weak, non-mechanistic predictor.
Late increased CVP monitoring may reflect ongoing congestion/low-output concerns, which are associated with AKI risk. However, frequency is still an indirect proxy and should not be weighted highly.

Mean EtCO2 in the immediate post-op window is heavily influenced by ventilator settings and transient anesthesia effects, making it nonspecific for renal perfusion. Collinearity-wise, extremes (especially low EtCO2) would better capture acute hypoperfusion than the mean.

Sustained lower mean EtCO2 can reflect reduced pulmonary blood flow/low cardiac output, indirectly associated with renal hypoperfusion. Still, mean is less sensitive than minima for detecting episodic low-flow states relevant to AKI.

In 25–36h, persistently low mean EtCO2 may indicate ongoing low cardiac output or poor perfusion, which can contribute to AKI. However, minima better capture clinically meaningful hypoperfusion episodes, so the mean is capped to reduce redundancy.

High EtCO2 is usually related to hypoventilation or increased CO2 production and is not a typical trigger for AKI. In 0–12h it is particularly confounded by ventilation/anesthesia and offers little renal-specific signal.
EtCO2 maxima are not a recognized driver of postoperative AKI and are often ventilator-management related. It provides limited information about renal perfusion compared with low EtCO2 extremes.
Even close to outcome, high EtCO2 is not a strong marker of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxic exposure. It is more reflective of ventilation strategy than kidney injury risk.

Low EtCO2 can indicate low cardiac output, pulmonary embolic phenomena, or severe hypotension/low pulmonary blood flow—states that can reduce renal perfusion. In 0–12h derangements are common and transient, so the score is conservatively capped.

A low EtCO2 minimum in 13–24h suggests ongoing or recurrent low-flow physiology (e.g., low cardiac output/shock), which is strongly linked to AKI via renal hypoperfusion. This extreme is more pathophysiologically relevant than mean/max for AKI prediction.

In 25–36h, a low EtCO2 minimum is a leading indicator of persistent/recurrent low cardiac output or severe hemodynamic compromise, a strong driver of postoperative AKI. It captures acute perfusion insults better than mean/max and is close to the 60h creatinine outcome.

EtCO2 measurement frequency reflects monitoring intensity (often continuous) rather than a physiologic mechanism for AKI. In the immediate post-op period it is routine and not specific for predicting creatinine rise.
Measurement frequency of EtCO2 mainly reflects monitoring intensity rather than renal physiology. At most it is a weak proxy for ongoing ventilatory/acuity concerns.
EtCO2 measurement count is a behavioral/monitoring signal and not a direct driver of AKI. Even close to hour 60 it is only a weak proxy for instability.

Higher average FiO2 can reflect respiratory failure and overall severity, which may correlate with AKI risk, but it is indirect. In the immediate post-op window this is often transient and protocol-driven.

Peak FiO2 early post-op can indicate acute hypoxemia/shock physiology and higher illness severity, which is associated with AKI. As an extreme it better captures acute insult than the mean, but in 0–12h scoring is capped.
Minimum FiO2 largely reflects weaning/ventilator strategy rather than a pathologic insult linked to AKI. It is not a meaningful predictor of renal injury.
FiO2 measurement frequency is routine in ventilated post-cardiac surgery patients and reflects documentation/monitoring rather than kidney perfusion. Weak proxy for acuity at best.
Counting FiO2 measurements is primarily a care-process variable and not mechanistically linked to AKI. It provides minimal incremental prognostic value beyond actual FiO2 levels.
FiO2 measurement frequency remains a monitoring intensity marker rather than a physiologic driver of creatinine rise. Close to outcome it may reflect concern but is still weak.

Mean tidal volume is mostly determined by ventilator protocol (e.g., lung-protective settings) and body size, with only indirect links to AKI via ventilator-induced lung injury/inflammation. In 0–12h it is unlikely to be a specific renal predictor.
Average tidal volume is generally protocolized and not a direct marker of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. Any association with AKI would be indirect and weak.
Sustained tidal volume settings are not a primary driver of postoperative AKI compared with hemodynamics, fluids, and nephrotoxins. It is an indirect severity/ventilation strategy marker at most.

Higher peak tidal volumes could reflect ventilator dyssynchrony or non–lung-protective ventilation, which may contribute to systemic inflammation and AKI risk, but evidence is indirect. As an extreme it is more informative than the mean, though early post-op effects are often transient.

Peak tidal volume may capture episodes of non–lung-protective ventilation or agitation, indirectly associated with AKI through inflammation/illness severity. It is not a strong or specific renal predictor.

Later peak tidal volumes may indicate ongoing respiratory failure or poor ventilator tolerance, correlating with severity and potential AKI risk, but remains indirect. Extreme values are more relevant than averages but still not a primary AKI driver.
Minimum tidal volume often reflects brief ventilator adjustments or spontaneous breathing/weaning rather than a harmful exposure. It has no clear mechanistic link to AKI.
Low minimum tidal volumes are typically due to ventilator strategy or transient changes and are not established predictors of renal injury. Any association with AKI would be weak and nonspecific.

Low tidal volumes can reflect lung-protective ventilation or reduced compliance/ARDS, which may correlate with overall severity and hypoxemia affecting renal perfusion. It is an indirect marker and not a primary AKI driver compared with hemodynamics or renal labs.
Measurement frequency is mainly a proxy for monitoring intensity rather than a physiologic mechanism for AKI. In the immediate post-op window it is routine and nonspecific.
This reflects clinician monitoring/ventilator management rather than a direct renal insult. It is not specific for impending AKI.
More frequent ventilator documentation may indicate ongoing respiratory instability/acuity closer to the outcome window. Still, it is a behavioral proxy and only indirectly related to AKI risk.
ABP pulse measurement presence/frequency is a monitoring artifact and common immediately post-cardiac surgery. It does not directly indicate renal hypoperfusion or injury.
This is primarily a proxy for continued invasive monitoring rather than a physiologic determinant of AKI. It is nonspecific for renal outcomes.
Continued ABP monitoring closer to hour 60 may reflect persistent hemodynamic concern and higher illness severity. However it remains an indirect behavioral marker rather than a direct AKI predictor.
Heart rate measurement frequency is routine in the immediate post-op period and reflects monitoring rather than physiology. It provides little specific signal for AKI risk.
This is a monitoring-intensity proxy and not a direct marker of renal perfusion or injury. It is unlikely to add specific predictive value for creatinine rise.
More frequent HR documentation may indicate ongoing instability (arrhythmia, shock) which can contribute to AKI risk. Still, as a _measured feature it is indirect and should be down-weighted.
MAP measurement frequency is standard after cardiac surgery and does not itself represent hypotension or renal hypoperfusion. As a behavioral proxy in 0–12h it is not informative for AKI.
This reflects monitoring rather than actual MAP values that drive renal perfusion. It is nonspecific for AKI trajectory.

Persistent close MAP monitoring near 25–36h may indicate concern for hemodynamic instability, which is relevant to AKI risk. Nonetheless, measurement frequency is indirect and should remain low importance.
Respiration measurement frequency is largely routine perioperative/ICU documentation and not a direct renal injury mechanism. In the immediate post-op period it is especially nonspecific.
This is a documentation/monitoring proxy rather than a physiologic driver of AKI. It provides minimal specific information about renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity.

More frequent respiratory monitoring later may reflect ongoing respiratory failure or sedation/ventilation needs, which can correlate with severity and AKI risk. Still, as a _measured feature it is indirect and low priority.
Measurement frequency reflects routine monitoring and clinician behavior rather than a renal mechanism. In the immediate post-op window it is nearly universal and not specific for AKI risk.
Still largely routine surveillance; ordering frequency is not a direct driver of renal injury. At most it weakly proxies overall acuity.
Pulse oximetry measurement frequency is not physiologically linked to creatinine rise and mainly reflects monitoring intensity. Not specific for renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity.
Counts of tube intake documentation/orders are a behavioral/recording proxy and not a direct determinant of renal perfusion. Early post-op feeding/NG use is common and nonspecific.
Measurement frequency is not a renal biomarker and only weakly reflects illness severity. Not a primary AKI predictor.
Even close to outcome, documentation frequency of tube intake is not mechanistically tied to AKI. At most it reflects care complexity rather than kidney injury.

IV fluid boluses can influence renal perfusion, but the mean bolus volume over 0–12h is a smoothed measure and early post-op resuscitation is common/transient. Extremes or later hemodynamic markers would be more informative.

A large maximum bolus suggests significant hypotension/vasoplegia or bleeding requiring resuscitation, which can precipitate renal hypoperfusion. Capped at 3 due to the 0–12h epoch where derangements are common and transient.
Minimum bolus volume is not clinically meaningful for AKI risk and adds redundancy relative to max/total resuscitation. It does not capture a pathologic insult.
Number of bolus entries/orders is a behavioral proxy for clinician concern and documentation, not a direct physiologic driver. In the immediate post-op period it is routine and nonspecific.

More frequent bolus administration/documentation in 13–24h may reflect ongoing instability (shock/bleeding) that increases AKI risk, but it remains an indirect behavioral proxy. Therefore limited to a low score.

Frequent bolus use close to hour 60 can indicate persistent hemodynamic instability associated with AKI, but measurement frequency is still indirect and collinear with actual volume/hemodynamics. Kept low per _measured rule.

Need for pacing can indicate conduction issues/low cardiac output states that may reduce renal perfusion, but early post-op pacing is common and often transient. Mean pacing over 0–12h is not a direct AKI marker.

Ongoing pacing requirement in the trajectory phase can reflect persistent cardiac dysfunction or low output, which is an established AKI risk factor via renal hypoperfusion. Still indirect and capped by epoch to moderate importance.

Persistent pacing requirement at 25–36h suggests ongoing hemodynamic compromise/low cardiac output, a strong driver of renal hypoperfusion and subsequent creatinine rise. This later window is a leading indicator for AKI risk.

Any pacing use (max) in the immediate post-op period is common after cardiac surgery and not specific for sustained low output. Extremes are less informative here than persistence into later epochs, so kept low.

Need for pacing suggests conduction disease/low cardiac output risk, which can impair renal perfusion, but it is an indirect marker and not kidney-specific. In this mid-phase window it has limited standalone predictive value for AKI.

Ongoing pacing requirement closer to hour 60 can indicate persistent hemodynamic compromise (e.g., low output/bradycardia) that reduces renal perfusion. Still indirect and confounded by routine post-op pacing practices.

Immediate post-op pacing is common and often transient after cardiac surgery, so it is a weak/indirect AKI signal in the initial period. It may reflect perioperative instability but is not specific for renal injury.

Continued pacing in this epoch may reflect ongoing cardiac dysfunction affecting renal blood flow, but remains a nonspecific proxy. Many patients are paced prophylactically, limiting specificity for AKI.

Persistent pacing requirement in the leading-indicator window can reflect sustained bradycardia/low output states that predispose to renal hypoperfusion. It is still an indirect marker rather than a renal biomarker.
Measurement frequency reflects monitoring/documentation behavior rather than physiology. In the immediate post-op period, frequent pacing documentation is routine and not specific for impending AKI.
This is primarily a care/monitoring intensity proxy and not a direct physiologic driver of kidney injury. It is unlikely to add specific AKI signal beyond whether pacing is present.

More frequent pacing-related measurements may indicate clinician concern about hemodynamic instability closer to the outcome, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still a behavioral proxy and should remain low importance.

Any CRRT/SLED-related maintenance implies severe illness and possible early renal dysfunction, but this variable is only measurement frequency, not actual therapy intensity. In 0–12h it may reflect perioperative instability and is capped low.

Ongoing CRRT/SLED maintenance documentation suggests significant renal/hemodynamic derangement, but the feature is a measurement-count proxy rather than a physiologic value. It may track acuity but is not a direct predictor.

CRRT/SLED maintenance activity close to hour 60 strongly implies severe AKI/critical illness, but this feature captures ordering/recording frequency rather than delivered dialysis dose. Therefore it remains low despite clinical face validity.

Sevoflurane exposure is not a strong established driver of post-cardiac surgery AKI compared with hemodynamics and nephrotoxins, and this is only a measurement proxy. In the immediate post-op period it largely reflects routine anesthesia documentation.
Measurement frequency of sevoflurane is a documentation artifact and not a renal mechanism. Continued recording may reflect sedation/anesthesia workflow rather than AKI risk.
This remains a behavioral/documentation proxy with weak mechanistic linkage to AKI. Prolonged anesthetic documentation is not a specific predictor of creatinine rise.
This is measurement frequency (not volume), reflecting charting intensity rather than fluid status. Early post-op intake documentation is routine and not specific for AKI risk.

Counting intake measurements is a weak proxy for acuity and does not directly represent fluid balance or renal perfusion. It is unlikely to add meaningful AKI signal beyond actual intake/output values.

Measurement frequency reflects clinician attention to fluid status/acuity rather than a direct renal mechanism. In the 25–36h window it may weakly proxy evolving hemodynamic instability or oliguria prompting closer I/O tracking.

How often drain output is recorded is largely routine post-cardiac surgery care and not a direct driver of AKI. In the immediate 0–12h period it mainly reflects standard monitoring rather than renal risk.

Drain output measurement frequency is a behavioral/monitoring variable with minimal physiologic specificity for kidney injury. At 13–24h it may reflect general acuity but is not an established AKI predictor.

More frequent drain checks late may indicate concern for bleeding/tamponade or instability that could reduce renal perfusion, but it remains an indirect proxy. As a measured-count feature it should not be weighted highly.
This appears to be an administrative/operational timestamp indicator rather than a physiologic exposure affecting renal perfusion. No meaningful mechanistic link to AKI risk.
Administrative arrival-time measurement does not capture hemodynamics, nephrotoxins, or renal function. Unlikely to add prognostic value for creatinine rise.
Administrative timing/measurement is not a renal biomarker and has no direct causal pathway to AKI. Any association would be spurious or site-workflow related.

Average time in sinus rhythm is an indirect marker of hemodynamic stability, but early post-op arrhythmias are common/transient and less specific for AKI. Mean aggregation also dilutes brief hypotensive/low-output episodes that matter more.

Persistent non-sinus rhythm can reduce cardiac output and renal perfusion, but the mean proportion in sinus rhythm remains an indirect marker. Mean aggregation is less informative than capturing episodes of instability directly.

By 25–36h, sustained failure to maintain sinus rhythm may reflect ongoing low-output state or atrial fibrillation burden that can impair renal perfusion. Still indirect and averaged, so not definitive.

A max indicator for being in sinus rhythm at any point is not clinically informative (most patients will have at least some sinus rhythm). It does not capture the harmful extreme (sustained arrhythmia) and is in the early transient period.
Having any sinus rhythm during the window (max) is a weak, non-specific marker and does not represent the pathologic extreme relevant to AKI. High redundancy with other rhythm summaries.

Max sinus rhythm remains uninformative because it ignores duration/burden of arrhythmia and hemodynamic impact. It is not a recognized predictor of AKI compared with measures of hypotension/vasopressor need.

A minimum of sinus rhythm (i.e., any period with no sinus rhythm) can indicate arrhythmia episodes that may compromise cardiac output and renal perfusion. In 0–12h this is common post-op, so capped conservatively.

If the minimum indicates sustained non-sinus rhythm at some point, it better captures the harmful extreme than mean/max and can reflect hemodynamic instability affecting kidneys. Still indirect and not a renal biomarker.

In the 25–36h leading window, any sustained absence of sinus rhythm suggests ongoing arrhythmia burden with potential low-output/hypoperfusion, a strong contributor to AKI risk. Among rhythm aggregations, the minimum best captures the pathologic extreme, reducing collinearity with mean/max.
Measurement frequency reflects monitoring intensity rather than renal physiology, and normal sinus rhythm itself is not an AKI driver. In the immediate post-op window this is especially nonspecific.
A behavioral proxy for monitoring/acuity rather than a mechanism for kidney injury. Presence of NSR monitoring does not directly predict creatinine rise.
Still primarily reflects how often rhythm status was documented rather than perfusion or nephrotoxicity. Not a direct predictor of creatinine_ratio.
Sinus variants are generally benign and do not reliably indicate hemodynamic compromise causing AKI. Mean over 0–12h further dilutes any transient instability.
Average burden of sinus variant rhythm is not an established AKI risk factor and is unlikely to reflect sustained low cardiac output. Mean aggregation is not capturing a specific renal insult.
Even close to the outcome window, sinus variant rhythm burden is not a strong marker of renal hypoperfusion. Mean aggregation is unlikely to add prognostic value for AKI.
A transient occurrence of sinus variant rhythm in the immediate post-op period is common and typically hemodynamically insignificant. Not a recognized trigger for AKI.
Max occurrence indicates any episode but sinus variants rarely cause meaningful hypotension or renal hypoperfusion. Weak link to creatinine_ratio.
Even if present in the leading-indicator window, sinus variant rhythm is not a strong correlate of low output or shock. Minimal expected predictive value for AKI.
Min (often indicating absence/lowest burden) is not clinically informative for AKI risk and is collinear with other rhythm summaries. No direct renal relevance.
Lowest burden/absence of sinus variant rhythm does not convey renal perfusion status. Not an AKI predictor.
Minimum burden is not a physiologic insult and adds little beyond other rhythm indicators. No meaningful mechanistic link to creatinine rise.
Measurement count is a documentation/monitoring proxy rather than a kidney injury mechanism. In 0–12h it is especially driven by routine post-op monitoring.
Frequency of noting sinus variant rhythm reflects clinician attention/telemetry review, not renal pathophysiology. Weak and indirect association at best.
Still a behavioral proxy; increased measurement may reflect general acuity but not specifically impending AKI. Per rules, measured features should remain low.

Atrial arrhythmias (e.g., AF) can reduce cardiac output and cause hypotension, increasing AKI risk, but early post-op episodes are common and often transient. Mean aggregation in 0–12h captures burden but this epoch is capped and less prognostic than later trajectory.
Atrial arrhythmias can worsen cardiac output and renal perfusion, but the mean burden is less informative than whether it occurred at all (max) and is collinear with it.
Later atrial arrhythmia burden may reflect ongoing hemodynamic instability, but presence/absence (max) better captures the clinically relevant insult; mean is capped to reduce redundancy.

Any atrial arrhythmia early after surgery can reduce forward flow and prompt vasoactive/diuretic changes that affect kidney perfusion, but this immediate period is often transient (max score capped at 3).
New or persistent atrial arrhythmia in the trajectory phase can signal ongoing instability and lower renal perfusion, moderately increasing AKI risk (epoch cap applies).
Atrial arrhythmia close to the outcome window can meaningfully impair cardiac output and renal blood flow and often co-occurs with shock/vasopressor needs, making it a strong predictor.
The minimum of a binary arrhythmia indicator is typically uninformative (often just reflects at least one timepoint without arrhythmia) and adds collinearity without capturing pathology.
Binary minimum does not represent arrhythmia burden or severity and is redundant with max/mean features.
Binary minimum is not clinically meaningful for AKI prediction and is largely a proxy for documentation structure rather than physiology.
Measurement frequency reflects monitoring/documentation intensity rather than a renal mechanism; early post-op monitoring is routine and not specific for AKI risk.
How often rhythm status is recorded is mainly a behavioral proxy and is not a direct driver of kidney injury.
Increased rhythm assessments later may reflect clinician concern for instability, which can correlate with AKI risk, but it remains an indirect behavioral marker.
Need for pacing can indicate conduction disease or low-output states, but mean pacing burden is less informative than whether pacing was required at all and early post-op pacing is common.
Ongoing pacing may correlate with cardiac dysfunction and reduced renal perfusion, but mean is a smoothed measure and likely collinear with binary indicators of pacing requirement.
Persistent pacing requirement closer to hour 60 can reflect sustained conduction/low-output problems that impair renal perfusion, giving moderate predictive value.
Any pacing in the immediate post-op period can mark hemodynamic vulnerability, but early pacing is often transient and protocol-driven (epoch cap at 3).
Requirement for pacing during 13–24h suggests ongoing instability or low-output physiology that can reduce renal perfusion, but it is not kidney-specific (epoch cap at 4, scored 3).

Need for pacing in the 25–36h window can reflect persistent conduction disease/low cardiac output physiology that may reduce renal perfusion and increase AKI risk. It is an indirect marker rather than a renal biomarker.

Early postoperative pacing is common and often transient after cardiac surgery, so it is a weak/indirect AKI signal in the 0–12h epoch. It may correlate with hemodynamic instability but is nonspecific.
Ongoing pacing requirement in 13–24h suggests slower recovery and possible hemodynamic compromise, which can contribute to AKI risk. Still indirect and not specific for renal injury.

Persistent pacing requirement close to the outcome window can indicate sustained conduction issues/low output state with potential renal hypoperfusion. Indirect but clinically meaningful in this later epoch.
Measurement frequency reflects monitoring/clinical attention rather than a physiologic mechanism of AKI. In 0–12h it is especially routine after cardiac surgery.
How often paced rhythm is documented is primarily a behavioral/monitoring artifact and not a direct driver of kidney injury. It adds little beyond the presence/absence of pacing.
More frequent documentation may reflect ongoing instability or clinician concern, which can correlate with AKI risk, but it remains an indirect behavioral proxy. Not a physiologic renal marker.

Average heart block burden in the immediate 0–12h period is often transient post-op and less predictive of sustained hypoperfusion-related AKI. Extremes/persistence later are more informative than the mean.
Mean heart block burden in 13–24h may indicate delayed recovery and potential hemodynamic effects, but averaging dilutes clinically important episodes. It is an indirect AKI predictor.

Sustained heart block could contribute to low cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion, but the mean is less specific than presence/episodes captured by max/min. To reduce collinearity, the mean is down-weighted.

Any episode of heart block in 0–12h can cause bradycardia/hypotension and transient renal hypoperfusion, but early post-op conduction issues are common and may resolve. Conservative scoring due to epoch.
Heart block episodes persisting into 13–24h suggest ongoing conduction pathology and potential hemodynamic compromise that can increase AKI risk. Still indirect and not kidney-specific.

Heart block episodes in 25–36h are a strong marker of persistent instability and risk for low cardiac output/hypotension, which directly threatens renal perfusion. This later timing makes it more predictive for creatinine rise by 60h.
Minimum (i.e., absence) of heart block in 0–12h is not informative for AKI risk and is largely expected in many patients. Extremes indicating presence are better captured by max.
Minimum values mainly reflect periods without heart block and do not capture the injurious episodes relevant to renal hypoperfusion. Max/presence is the more pathologic aggregation.

Minimum heart block in 25–36h largely indicates no heart block at some point and is not a strong AKI signal. Presence/episodes (max) better represent the pathologic trigger, so min is down-weighted for collinearity.
Measurement frequency reflects monitoring/concern rather than a direct renal mechanism. Early post-op conduction issues are common and transient; this is at best an indirect AKI signal.
Still a behavioral proxy for acuity/monitoring rather than physiology. Heart block may correlate with low output, but the 'measured' count is not a strong predictor.
Later persistent concern for heart block can imply ongoing hemodynamic instability that threatens renal perfusion, but measurement count remains indirect. Kept low per _measured rule.

Sustained ischemic changes can indicate myocardial ischemia/low cardiac output that predisposes to AKI, but in the immediate 0–12h window ST changes may be transient/post-bypass. Mean also smooths brief insults.
Ongoing ischemia can contribute to renal hypoperfusion, but the mean aggregation is less specific than an extreme/any-episode indicator. Capped to reduce collinearity with max/min versions.
Closer to outcome, persistent ischemia could matter, but mean remains a diluted signal compared with max/min (any episode). Capped for collinearity control.

Any ischemic ST change (max) suggests myocardial ischemia and potential low-output state, a recognized AKI risk pathway. In 0–12h, however, peri-bypass artifacts/transient changes are common so capped at 3.

Ischemic ST changes in the trajectory phase more strongly suggest true ongoing myocardial ischemia/low cardiac output, which directly threatens renal perfusion. Max captures acute episodes better than mean.
Late ischemic ST changes are a strong marker of ongoing cardiac ischemia/instability and likely reduced renal perfusion, increasing AKI risk. Max best captures clinically meaningful episodes.
For a binary ischemia indicator, min is less informative (often reflects absence at some point) and is redundant with max/mean. In the immediate post-op window it is particularly nonspecific.
Min is a weak/collinear summary for a binary ischemia feature and does not capture the presence of ischemic episodes as well as max. Kept low to avoid redundancy.
Even late, min is not the best aggregation for detecting ischemic insults and is largely redundant with max. Low importance to reduce collinearity.
Number of measurements reflects clinician attention/monitoring rather than a physiologic driver of AKI. Early post-op ECG scrutiny is routine and not specific for renal injury.
More frequent assessment may indicate concern for ischemia/hemodynamic instability, which can correlate with AKI risk, but it remains an indirect behavioral proxy. Scored low per _measured rule.
Late increased monitoring for ischemia may reflect ongoing instability that can impair renal perfusion, but measurement frequency is still indirect. Kept at 2 per rule.

Non-specific rhythm abnormalities can correlate with hemodynamic instability and vasopressor need, indirectly affecting renal perfusion. Mean in the immediate 0–12h period is nonspecific and likely collinear with more direct hemodynamic features.
Non-sinus/other rhythms can correlate with hemodynamic instability and renal hypoperfusion, but the mean over 12h is a nonspecific summary and less informative than discrete episodes.
Persistent ‘other’ rhythm later may reflect ongoing instability, but a mean aggregation is still nonspecific and likely collinear with episode-based indicators.

Any occurrence of an ‘other’ rhythm immediately post-op can indicate acute arrhythmia-related low cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion, though early post-bypass arrhythmias are often transient (0–12h cap).
An episode of ‘other’ rhythm in the trajectory phase can signal ongoing arrhythmia/hemodynamic compromise that increases AKI risk, but it is not kidney-specific.
Late (25–36h) occurrence of an ‘other’ rhythm suggests persistent or recurrent instability closer to the creatinine outcome window, increasing likelihood of renal hypoperfusion and AKI.

Continued ASV use may reflect ongoing respiratory support needs and overall severity, but it is an indirect and nonspecific predictor of AKI.
Any ASV use early post-op is common and reflects ventilatory management rather than renal physiology; at most it weakly proxies severity (0–12h conservative).
ASV use in 13–24h may indicate delayed extubation/greater severity, which can associate with AKI, but it is not a direct renal risk factor.

Measurement frequency reflects clinician behavior/documentation rather than a renal mechanism. In the immediate 0–12h post-op period, ventilator mode checks are routine and not specific for AKI risk.

Counts of ASV documentation/orders are a weak proxy for acuity and are not a direct driver of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. Per rules, _measured features should be low unless strongly tied to AKI suspicion.

Controlled ventilation early post-cardiac surgery is common and mainly reflects immediate post-op management rather than renal insult. Any AKI link is indirect through severity/sedation/hemodynamics, and 0–12h is capped conservatively.

Persistent controlled ventilation into 13–24h can indicate slower recovery and higher illness severity, indirectly associated with AKI. As a mean/average indicator of mode, it remains nonspecific for renal perfusion injury.

Any use of controlled mode in the first 12h is expected after surgery and not specific for kidney injury. It may weakly track severity and need for deep sedation/vasopressors, hence only indirect relevance.

Use of controlled ventilation at any point in 13–24h suggests ongoing respiratory failure or hemodynamic instability, which can contribute to renal hypoperfusion. This is still indirect but more informative than early post-op use.

A minimum/always-on indicator of controlled mode in 0–12h largely reflects routine immediate post-op ventilation strategy. It provides little discrimination for AKI risk in this early transient period.

Being on controlled ventilation throughout 13–24h implies persistent critical illness and potentially higher PEEP/sedation/vasopressor needs, which can worsen renal perfusion. This is a stronger severity proxy than intermittent use.
Frequency of documenting/ordering controlled mode is behavioral and routine in the immediate post-op window. It is not a physiologic marker of AKI and should be scored low.
_measured features primarily capture monitoring intensity rather than renal pathophysiology. Even if higher in sicker patients, it remains a weak and nonspecific proxy.

Late increased measurement frequency may reflect ongoing ventilatory instability and higher acuity closer to the creatinine outcome window. Still, it is not a direct renal mechanism and remains a weak predictor.
SIMV use early post-op is common and reflects ventilator weaning strategy more than renal perfusion status. Any association with AKI is minimal and indirect in the 0–12h period.

SIMV in 13–24h may indicate partial recovery/weaning versus ongoing respiratory failure, indirectly correlating with overall severity and AKI risk. As a mean indicator of mode, it remains nonspecific.
Any SIMV use in the first 12h is largely a routine ventilator management choice after surgery. It has no direct mechanistic link to AKI and offers limited prognostic value.

SIMV use can proxy ongoing respiratory failure/sedation needs and illness severity, which may correlate with AKI risk. As a ventilator-mode indicator (and using an extreme aggregation), it is indirect and not a primary renal mechanism.

Spontaneous modes may indicate earlier recovery and less need for deep sedation/vasopressors, indirectly associated with lower AKI risk. In 0–12h this is often transient and protocol-driven, so conservative scoring applies.

More time in spontaneous mode can reflect improving cardiopulmonary status and less critical illness, indirectly lowering AKI risk. As an averaged ventilator-mode feature, it remains an indirect marker.
Any spontaneous breathing in the first 12h may signal faster stabilization, indirectly associated with less AKI risk. However, early post-op extubation practices vary and are not kidney-specific.

Presence of spontaneous mode by 13–24h can indicate successful weaning and less ongoing shock/organ dysfunction, which is more informative for AKI trajectory than early post-op. Still, it is an indirect severity marker rather than a renal biomarker.
The minimum spontaneous-mode value (often zero) is not a physiologic insult and is largely determined by immediate post-op management. It has minimal specific linkage to AKI.
Minimum spontaneous-mode exposure provides little incremental information beyond whether spontaneous breathing occurred at all. It is not a direct predictor of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity.
Measurement frequency is a documentation/monitoring proxy and not a physiologic driver. In the immediate post-op window it is routine and not AKI-specific.
How often spontaneous mode is recorded reflects workflow rather than kidney risk. Any association with AKI would be indirect and weak.

Mean arterial pressure relates directly to renal perfusion; sustained hypotension increases AKI risk after cardiac surgery. Because this is a 0–12h mean (and early post-op fluctuations are common), it is capped conservatively and extremes would be more informative than the mean.

MAP relates to renal perfusion, but the mean over 12h can mask hypotensive episodes that drive AKI; the MAP_min is the more pathophysiologic aggregation. In the 13–24h window, use conservatively to avoid collinearity with extremes.

Hypertensive peaks are not a typical direct trigger for postoperative AKI compared with hypotension/low perfusion. Early (0–12h) values are often transient and treatment-related.
MAP maxima generally reflect vasopressor titration/pain rather than renal hypoperfusion risk. Not a strong mechanistic predictor of creatinine rise compared with MAP_min.
High MAP episodes are not a primary driver of AKI in this setting; low MAP is the key insult. Max is also collinear with other MAP summaries without adding renal-specific signal.

Hypotension is a known contributor to renal ischemia after cardiac surgery, and the minimum MAP captures acute low-perfusion insults. Score capped by the 0–12h epoch where transient post-bypass hypotension is common.

Persistent or recurrent hypotension in the 13–24h trajectory phase strongly predicts evolving renal hypoperfusion and AKI. The minimum MAP best captures clinically meaningful insults compared with mean/max.

Measurement frequency reflects monitoring intensity rather than physiology, and arterial lines are routine post-cardiac surgery. In 0–12h it mainly indicates standard care rather than AKI risk.

NPO status early after cardiac surgery is routine and not mechanistically linked to AKI. It mainly reflects postoperative workflow rather than renal perfusion or nephrotoxin exposure.

Binary NPO in the immediate postoperative period is expected standard care and provides little discrimination for AKI risk. Not a physiologic marker of renal injury.
Being NPO at any point in 13–24h is common and nonspecific; it may reflect routine extubation/feeding timing rather than kidney risk. Weak indirect association at best.

Persistent NPO status late (25–36h) can be an indirect marker of ongoing critical illness, delayed extubation, or hemodynamic instability that may increase AKI risk. It is not a direct physiologic driver of creatinine rise.

NPO status in 13–24h is still commonly protocol- or workflow-driven and only weakly reflects renal risk. Any association with AKI would be indirect via overall acuity.

How often NPO status is recorded is primarily a workflow artifact and not a renal perfusion marker. At most it weakly tracks acuity.

Average diet status in 0–12h is largely determined by standard postoperative care and does not capture a kidney-relevant insult. It is unlikely to be causally linked to creatinine rise.
Mean diet status in 13–24h is a nonspecific recovery marker and not a direct determinant of renal injury. Any relationship to AKI would be indirect and weak.

Failure to advance diet by 25–36h can indicate ongoing critical illness or complications associated with AKI risk. As an averaged/summary measure, it remains indirect and potentially collinear with NPO indicators.
Having any diet intake in 0–12h is uncommon and mostly reflects protocol variation rather than renal physiology. Early feeding status is not a recognized AKI predictor.
Ability to tolerate diet by 13–24h may indicate improving clinical status, indirectly associated with lower AKI risk. It is not a direct renal biomarker.
Diet tolerance by 25–36h suggests recovery and less severe illness, which may correlate with lower AKI risk. Still an indirect marker and not kidney-specific.
Minimum diet status in 0–12h largely reflects routine NPO immediately after surgery and adds little AKI-specific information. It is expected and not pathologic.
Minimum diet status in 13–24h is still commonly NPO for non-renal reasons and is a weak, indirect proxy for acuity. It is not a primary AKI driver.
Persistently minimal/no diet in 25–36h can reflect ongoing instability or complications that increase AKI risk. However, it is indirect and potentially redundant with NPO features.

Measurement frequency of diet orders is a care-process marker and not a physiologic driver of AKI. In the immediate 0–12h post-op period it is unlikely to add specific prognostic value for creatinine rise.
Diet order frequency mainly reflects workflow/acuity rather than renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity. Weak and nonspecific association with subsequent creatinine ratio.

More frequent diet-related documentation/orders late may reflect ongoing instability or delayed feeding, which can correlate with illness severity. Still indirect and behavioral, so limited predictive value for AKI.

Any occurrence of an 'other' diet order in 0–12h is common and largely protocol-driven (e.g., NPO), not kidney-specific. Weak link to creatinine trajectory.

Having any 'other' diet status in the 25–36h window may reflect delayed extubation/ileus/ongoing instability, indirectly correlating with AKI risk. Still nonspecific and not causal.

Frequency of documenting/ordering an 'other' diet is a behavioral/process variable, not a physiologic AKI driver. In 0–12h it is especially protocolized and nonspecific.
Measurement frequency reflects clinician workflow and general acuity rather than kidney injury. Weak and indirect association at best.
More frequent diet-status changes/orders late may indicate ongoing complications and higher illness severity, which can correlate with AKI. Still indirect and should remain low importance.

Cardiac rhythm regularity relates indirectly to renal perfusion (arrhythmias can reduce cardiac output), but in 0–12h transient rhythm changes are common post-op. Mean aggregation may miss brief high-impact arrhythmias, so importance is capped.

Mean proportion of “regular” rhythm is an indirect proxy for absence of arrhythmia and does not directly reflect renal perfusion. Prefer irregularity extremes/occurrence over averaged regularity to avoid collinearity.

Any regular rhythm in 25–36h is not a marker of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. The clinically relevant signal would be irregularity/arrhythmia rather than regularity.

Recording frequency is not a physiologic marker of renal injury and is often standard ICU monitoring. At most it reflects general instability, so low importance.

Irregular rhythm in this trajectory phase may reflect evolving instability but remains indirect for AKI compared with direct perfusion markers. Scored conservatively given potential collinearity with other irregularity summaries.

Counts of measurements are primarily a behavioral proxy for acuity/monitoring intensity, not a direct driver of renal injury. Rhythm monitoring remains standard in this phase.

More frequent rhythm assessments late may indicate clinician concern for instability, which can correlate with AKI risk, but it is still indirect and non-physiologic. Kept low per the measured-feature rule.

An 'other' rhythm category is heterogeneous and hard to interpret mechanistically for renal perfusion, especially as a mean in the immediate post-op window. Likely reflects documentation noise more than AKI biology.

Late 'other' rhythm could capture clinically relevant dysrhythmias or pacing states that affect perfusion, but the category is too heterogeneous to be a strong predictor. Mean aggregation further dilutes acute events.

Any occurrence of a non-standard rhythm early could reflect transient pacing/ectopy or conduction issues, which may relate to hemodynamic swings, but early post-op effects are often temporary. Max is preferred over mean/min for capturing an acute event.

Occurrence of an 'other' rhythm in this phase may indicate ongoing conduction/rhythm issues with potential perfusion impact, but remains non-specific. Max captures the event better than mean/min but is still indirect for AKI.

In the 25–36h window, any occurrence of an atypical rhythm/pacing state may signal persistent cardiac dysfunction that can impair renal perfusion and contribute to AKI. Max best captures the presence of such an insult compared with mean/min.
The minimum of a binary 'other rhythm' indicator is generally uninformative and highly collinear with max/any-occurrence. Early post-op documentation variability further limits interpretability.
Binary-min aggregation provides little clinical meaning (often just indicates there was some time without 'other' rhythm) and is redundant with max. Not a direct or established AKI predictor.

As a binary-min summary it is not a good representation of pathologic exposure and is collinear with the max feature. Even late, it does not capture severity or duration relevant to renal hypoperfusion.

Measurement frequency is mainly a proxy for monitoring intensity rather than renal physiology, and early post-op rhythm checks are routine. In the 0–12h window it is especially nonspecific for later AKI.
Still primarily reflects clinician attention/acuity rather than a direct mechanism for AKI. Rhythm assessment frequency is not a reliable independent predictor of creatinine rise.

Increased rhythm-related monitoring late may reflect hemodynamic instability (e.g., atrial fibrillation) that can reduce renal perfusion, but it remains an indirect behavioral proxy. Therefore it should stay low.
Mean HR in the immediate post-op period is influenced by pain, temperature, and inotropes and is often transient. It is only an indirect marker of hemodynamic stress relevant to AKI.

Sustained tachycardia can indicate ongoing stress/low stroke volume that may impair renal perfusion, but the mean smooths important extremes. As an average it is less specific than max/min for AKI risk.

Persistent abnormal HR closer to hour 60 can reflect ongoing shock, arrhythmia burden, or inadequate cardiac output affecting renal perfusion. Still, mean HR is less informative than extremes for acute insults.
Early extreme tachycardia can signal bleeding, pain/agitation, or low cardiac output states that threaten renal perfusion. However, in 0–12h it is common and transient, so capped at 3.

Low HR extremes may indicate conduction disease or medication effects leading to low cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion. As an extreme it is more relevant than mean but not definitive.

Late bradycardia extremes can be a strong marker of low cardiac output/hemodynamic compromise, which directly threatens renal perfusion and increases AKI risk. Extremes capture the insult better than averages.

Later sustained HR elevation may indicate persistent hemodynamic stress associated with AKI risk, but the mean is less informative than max/min for acute insults and is nonspecific.

Persistent/recurrent tachycardia in the trajectory phase can reflect ongoing low output or sepsis-like physiology that increases AKI risk, though it remains indirect.

Mechanical ventilation early post-op reflects illness severity and potential hemodynamic/oxygenation stress, but in 0–12h it is often routine after cardiac surgery. As a _measured count it is also a care-intensity proxy rather than a direct AKI mechanism.

Ongoing need for mechanical ventilation into 13–24h suggests slower recovery and higher acuity, which can correlate with AKI risk. However, _measured is a behavioral proxy and not a direct renal perfusion marker.

Being on no oxygen device in the immediate post-op period is not a direct driver of renal injury and is heavily influenced by extubation practices. The mean over 0–12h is also less informative than whether the patient ever required support.

Persistent need for low-flow oxygen late may reflect ongoing cardiopulmonary dysfunction that can indirectly worsen renal perfusion. However, it is nonspecific and less informative than hemodynamics/vasopressors or hypoxemia extremes.

Immediate post-op oxygen device selection is common and heavily influenced by routine extubation/weaning practices rather than kidney injury mechanisms. In the 0–12h epoch, this is a weak and transient marker.

Low-flow oxygen use in the 25–36h window may indicate incomplete cardiopulmonary recovery, which can correlate with renal hypoperfusion risk. Still, it is nonspecific and not a direct AKI biomarker.

Minimum low-flow use (i.e., whether low-flow was present at all) in the immediate post-op period mainly reflects routine oxygen supplementation. It has no direct physiologic linkage to AKI and is highly practice-pattern dependent.

Counts of recorded device status are primarily a charting intensity proxy and not a physiologic driver of AKI. It is unlikely to indicate targeted concern for renal injury.

High-flow oxygen early can indicate significant respiratory compromise and higher overall illness severity, which may indirectly increase AKI risk. In 0–12h, however, respiratory support needs are often transient and perioperative, so importance is capped low.

Ongoing high-flow oxygen requirement in 13–24h suggests persistent cardiopulmonary dysfunction and potential low cardiac output/hypoxemia, both associated with AKI risk. As a mean/usage measure it is still less specific than extremes of hypoxemia or vasopressor need.

Any high-flow use in the immediate post-op period can reflect early respiratory failure severity, indirectly linked to AKI via hypoxemia and hemodynamic stress. But early post-op variability is common, so predictive value is limited.

Mean ALT in the first 12 hours is a nonspecific marker and averages dilute acute hepatic ischemia; it has weak and indirect linkage to AKI compared with hemodynamics and renal labs.

An early ALT spike can indicate ischemic hepatitis/low-flow state after surgery, which correlates with systemic hypoperfusion and higher AKI risk, though it is not kidney-specific and early period limits strength.
ALT minima are not clinically meaningful for AKI risk and do not capture the hypoperfusion-related injury signal (which is reflected by maxima).
ALT ordering frequency reflects clinician concern or routine postoperative panels rather than a direct physiologic pathway to AKI.
Repeated ALT checks are primarily a care-process marker and only weakly proxy severity; they are not a direct predictor of creatinine rise.
Late repeated ALT testing may indicate ongoing shock/liver injury concern and overall illness severity, but it remains an indirect behavioral proxy rather than a renal biomarker.
BUN relates to renal function and catabolic state, but early postoperative values are confounded by hemodilution, transfusion, and fluid shifts; mean further smooths extremes, limiting specificity.
BUN in the trajectory phase can reflect evolving renal dysfunction or prerenal azotemia from low effective circulating volume, providing moderate predictive value for later creatinine rise.
In the closest window to the outcome, elevated mean BUN more strongly signals developing renal impairment/prerenal physiology and is a strong predictor of subsequent creatinine increase by hour 60.
Elevated BUN can reflect reduced renal clearance or hypoperfusion, but in the immediate post-CPB period it is often transient/hemodilution-related; capped by 0–12h max score limit.
Rising BUN in the trajectory phase can indicate evolving renal dysfunction or catabolic stress and is a moderate AKI risk signal, though less direct than creatinine/urine output.
Late (25–36h) BUN elevation is closer to the outcome window and more consistent with impaired renal clearance or sustained hypoperfusion, making it a strong predictor of higher creatinine_ratio.
Low BUN is usually driven by hemodilution/low protein intake and is not a meaningful AKI signal, especially immediately post-op.
A low BUN in this window is generally not pathognomonic for AKI and provides little prognostic information for creatinine rise.
Low BUN late is not a typical marker of impending AKI and is more reflective of dilutional state or low urea generation.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine post-cardiac surgery lab protocols and clinician behavior rather than renal physiology.
More frequent BUN checks may reflect concern for renal dysfunction/volume status, but it is an indirect behavioral proxy rather than a mechanism.
Increased ordering late may indicate escalating acuity or suspected AKI, but remains an indirect marker and should be low-weighted.
Amylase testing relates to pancreatitis/abdominal pathology and is not a standard AKI predictor; ordering early is unlikely to add renal-specific signal.
Amylase measurement is not kidney-specific and typically reflects evaluation for pancreatitis or ischemia rather than AKI risk.
Even late, amylase ordering is a nonspecific behavioral marker and has weak linkage to postoperative AKI compared with hemodynamics and renal labs.
Average pH early is influenced by transient perioperative acid-base shifts; sustained severe acidosis is more informative than the mean in this window.
Persistently low average pH can reflect ongoing shock/lactic acidosis and is associated with renal hypoperfusion, giving moderate AKI relevance.
Ongoing acidemia close to hour 60 suggests persistent hypoperfusion/organ dysfunction and is strongly associated with subsequent creatinine rise.
Alkalemia extremes are generally less directly linked to AKI than acidemia; early post-op pH highs often reflect ventilation/bicarbonate and are not renal-specific.

Alkalemia is usually not a primary driver of AKI; pH extremes matter more on the acidemic side. Using max is less pathophysiologically relevant than pH minima for renal hypoperfusion/poor perfusion states.

Late alkalemia may reflect ventilation/diuresis but is not a strong direct predictor of AKI compared with acidemia. Max pH is generally less informative than minimum pH for shock/ischemia-related kidney injury.

Early postoperative acidemia can indicate low cardiac output, hypoperfusion, or high lactate burden, all linked to AKI risk. However, in the immediate post-CPB period derangements are common/transient, so capped at 3.

Persistent or recurrent acidemia in the trajectory phase suggests ongoing hypoperfusion/shock or severe respiratory/metabolic failure, which strongly increases AKI risk. Minimum pH captures the acute insult better than mean/max.

Acidemia close to the outcome window is a strong marker of ongoing systemic illness and impaired perfusion, both tightly linked to subsequent creatinine rise. The minimum pH best captures clinically meaningful extremes relevant to AKI.

More frequent blood gas checks reflect acuity/instability and clinician concern rather than a direct renal mechanism. In the immediate postoperative period frequent sampling is common, limiting specificity for AKI.
Higher measurement frequency may indicate ongoing instability (ventilation/hemodynamics) and thus indirectly higher AKI risk. Still primarily a behavior/acuity proxy rather than a physiologic driver.
Late frequent blood gas monitoring suggests persistent critical illness and may correlate with AKI risk, but it is not mechanistic. As a utilization proxy it should remain low importance.

Cholesterol testing is not part of AKI physiology and is rarely clinically indicated in the immediate post-cardiac surgery ICU course. Measurement mainly reflects routine/history-taking rather than renal risk.

Ordering cholesterol in this window is unlikely to relate to evolving AKI and provides minimal prognostic information for creatinine rise. It is largely unrelated to perioperative renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity.
Cholesterol measurement late post-op is not a meaningful indicator of impending AKI and is not a renal biomarker. Any association would be incidental or confounded by care patterns.

Lymphopenia can reflect stress/inflammation and overall illness severity, which may correlate with AKI risk indirectly. Mean values are less informative than extremes and early post-op changes are often nonspecific.
Sustained lymphopenia may indicate ongoing systemic inflammation/sepsis risk, indirectly associated with AKI. As a mean aggregation it is a weaker signal than minima and not kidney-specific.
High lymphocyte counts are not a recognized trigger or marker for AKI in this setting. Max values are unlikely to capture relevant pathology compared with lymphocyte minima (stress lymphopenia).
Maximum lymphocyte count has little physiologic linkage to AKI risk after cardiac surgery. It is more likely noise/collinear with other inflammatory markers than a meaningful predictor.

Marked early lymphopenia can reflect severe physiologic stress/inflammation and higher overall postoperative acuity, which is associated with AKI risk. In the immediate 0–12h period it remains nonspecific, so capped at 3.

Lymphopenia can reflect stress/inflammation and overall illness severity, which correlates indirectly with AKI risk. The minimum value is not a specific renal-perfusion marker and is less directly linked to creatinine rise.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects ordering behavior/acuity rather than a physiologic driver of AKI. In the immediate 0–12h post-op period it is especially nonspecific.
This is a behavioral proxy for clinician concern and does not directly indicate renal injury. It is not specific for impending creatinine rise.
More frequent checks late may indicate evolving complications/sepsis concern, which can precede AKI. Still, it is an indirect, non-physiologic proxy so capped low.
Whether glucose was measured is largely routine ICU practice and reflects monitoring intensity rather than kidney injury. In 0–12h it is particularly standard-of-care.
Glucose measurement frequency is nonspecific and mostly reflects protocolized care. It has no direct mechanistic link to AKI beyond general acuity.
Late glucose monitoring may increase with instability, insulin infusions, or infection concern, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still an indirect behavioral marker, so low importance.

Ordering CK may reflect concern for rhabdomyolysis/ischemia, which can contribute to AKI, but measurement frequency is not a physiologic value. Early post-op ordering is often precautionary, limiting specificity.
CK ordering in this window may indicate suspected muscle injury/low-flow states that can predispose to AKI. However it remains an ordering-behavior proxy rather than a direct biomarker.
Late CK checks can signal ongoing concern for rhabdomyolysis or ischemic injury, which can precede creatinine rise. Still, as a measured-count feature it is capped at low importance.

Lower eGFR reflects reduced renal function and is related to subsequent creatinine rise, but in 0–12h it can be transiently distorted by perioperative fluid shifts and creatinine kinetics. Mean eGFR is less sensitive to acute insults than a nadir/min would be.

Sustained reduction in eGFR during the trajectory phase suggests evolving renal dysfunction and is a strong predictor of later creatinine elevation. Mean captures persistent impairment over the window, though still derived from creatinine.

In the closest pre-outcome window, a low mean eGFR strongly indicates established renal dysfunction and is highly predictive of creatinine_ratio at 60h. It is effectively an early creatinine-based marker of AKI progression.
The maximum eGFR reflects the best (least impaired) renal estimate and is not the pathologic signal for AKI risk. Also redundant with mean eGFR, so kept minimal to reduce collinearity.
Peak eGFR is not informative for AKI risk compared with lower/average values and is collinear with eGFR_mean. It does not capture renal insult.
Maximum eGFR in this window reflects transiently better creatinine estimates and does not represent kidney injury. It is redundant with eGFR_mean and not the relevant direction for AKI prediction.

Low eGFR reflects reduced renal filtration and is closely tied to creatinine rise, but in the immediate 0–12h post-CPB period transient shifts and dilution are common (cap at 3). The minimum value best captures early renal insult vs mean/measured.

Persistently low nadir eGFR in 13–24h suggests evolving renal dysfunction beyond immediate postoperative noise and is a strong predictor of later creatinine rise. Minimum captures the clinically relevant insult better than mean.

A low eGFR nadir close to the 60h outcome is essentially an early biomarker of impaired filtration and strongly predicts creatinine_ratio. This is the most proximal and pathophysiologically direct signal among eGFR aggregates.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects clinician concern/acuity rather than renal physiology. Early postoperative labs are routine, so ordering count has limited specificity for impending AKI.

More frequent eGFR/chemistry checks may indicate concern for instability or renal issues, but it is a behavioral proxy and not a direct mechanism. Keep low to avoid over-weighting practice-pattern effects.
Increased measurement frequency late may reflect suspected AKI and closer monitoring, but remains indirect and confounded by ICU practice. Score kept low per measured-feature rule.

LDH ordering frequency is a nonspecific marker of illness/workup (e.g., hemolysis, ischemia) and not directly linked to renal filtration. In 0–12h it is often routine/confirmatory, offering little AKI-specific signal.
LDH measurement count reflects clinician behavior and nonspecific concern (hemolysis/ischemia) rather than kidney injury. Limited specificity for predicting creatinine_ratio.
Even late, LDH ordering frequency is an indirect, nonspecific acuity proxy and not a renal biomarker. Weak mechanistic link to AKI compared with hemodynamics/renal labs.

Average INR early post-op reflects coagulation status and liver function/warfarin effect; it is only indirectly related to AKI via bleeding/transfusion or shock. Mean is less informative than extremes for acute complications (cap at 2).

Sustained INR elevation may correlate with hepatic dysfunction/bleeding risk and overall severity, but is not a primary AKI driver. Mean is less pathologically specific than INR extremes for acute bleeding/coagulopathy.

A high INR peak can signal significant coagulopathy/bleeding risk leading to hypotension/transfusion and renal hypoperfusion, but early post-CPB coagulopathy is common and transient (cap at 3). Max better captures clinically relevant derangement than mean/min.

Late INR spikes may indicate ongoing coagulopathy, hepatic dysfunction, or anticoagulation issues associated with bleeding/hemodynamic instability that can precipitate AKI. Still indirect compared with renal/hemodynamic markers, so moderate importance.
Low INR is generally not a trigger for AKI and is less clinically relevant than high INR for bleeding-related renal hypoperfusion. Minimum adds little beyond other coagulation features.
A low INR late is not a recognized AKI risk factor and is typically clinically reassuring rather than harmful. Minimal mechanistic connection to creatinine rise.

INR measurement frequency is largely protocol-driven after cardiac surgery and reflects monitoring practices more than renal pathophysiology. As a behavioral proxy, it has weak AKI-specific predictive value.

Frequency of INR checks reflects bleeding/anticoagulation management and overall acuity rather than a direct AKI mechanism. Could correlate indirectly with shock/transfusion needs that affect renal perfusion.

More frequent INR monitoring late may indicate ongoing bleeding, liver dysfunction, or anticoagulation complexity, which can track with critical illness. Still a behavioral proxy and not a direct renal injury marker.

Eosinophil percentage is not a typical driver or early marker of post-cardiac surgery AKI, and early postoperative leukocyte shifts are nonspecific. Mean values in this immediate period are unlikely to add prognostic signal.

Average eosinophil percentage remains a weak, nonspecific inflammatory/allergic signal with little established link to ischemic/ATN-type AKI after cardiac surgery. Mean aggregation further dilutes any transient signal.

A spike in eosinophils could rarely suggest drug reaction/atheroembolic phenomena, but this is uncommon and early postoperative changes are often noise. In 0–12h, cap applies and clinical linkage to AKI is indirect.

An elevated maximum eosinophil percentage could weakly indicate hypersensitivity/interstitial nephritis risk, but this is not a common pathway for early post-cardiac surgery AKI. Best interpreted as a nonspecific inflammatory signal.
Low eosinophil percentage is common with stress response and has no meaningful mechanistic link to AKI. Minimum values are not a recognized trigger or marker for renal injury.
Minimum eosinophil percentage mainly reflects stress leukogram/catecholamine effect and is not informative for AKI prediction. No established association with renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity.
Measurement count reflects CBC ordering frequency and general monitoring rather than renal pathophysiology. In the immediate postoperative window, this is routine and not specific to AKI concern.
CBC/eosinophil measurement frequency is largely standard ICU practice and a weak proxy for acuity. It does not directly indicate impending AKI.
Even late, eosinophil measurement frequency is more about monitoring behavior than kidney injury mechanisms. It is not typically ordered specifically to evaluate AKI risk in this context.
LDL testing is unrelated to acute renal perfusion or tubular injury and is not part of AKI evaluation. Ordering in 0–12h is likely incidental or baseline risk profiling.
LDL measurement does not reflect hemodynamics, nephrotoxicity, or renal function trajectory. Any association with AKI would be confounded and indirect.
LDL testing late post-op is not clinically tied to AKI prediction and is unlikely to carry meaningful signal for creatinine rise. Primarily reflects non-renal care processes.

MCV reflects chronic anemia/nutritional status and can correlate with frailty, but it is not a direct AKI driver. In 0–12h, mean values are unlikely to capture acute renal insults and are capped conservatively.

MCV remains an indirect marker (baseline hematologic status, transfusion history) with weak linkage to renal hypoperfusion/ATN. Mean aggregation provides limited incremental information for AKI trajectory.

MCV is not a direct AKI marker; it may indirectly reflect anemia/transfusion or chronic nutritional status that can affect oxygen delivery. Mean values are less informative than acute extremes for perioperative insults.
Early postoperative MCV elevations are usually dilution/transfusion-related and not a primary AKI driver. In the 0–12h epoch, transient shifts are common and weakly predictive.
MCV max in this window may reflect ongoing transfusion or hemoconcentration but has only an indirect relationship to renal injury. Not an established predictor of creatinine rise.
Later MCV extremes could signal hemoconcentration/dehydration or transfusion effects, which can influence renal perfusion indirectly. Still nonspecific and not a direct AKI biomarker.
Low MCV may reflect anemia/hemodilution after bypass, which can reduce oxygen delivery but is not a direct AKI indicator. Conservative scoring due to immediate post-op variability.
Persistently low MCV suggests anemia/hemodilution and possible transfusion needs, indirectly affecting renal oxygenation. Association with AKI is weak and nonspecific.
